articles.title: Mars dust may be less abrasive than lunar dust, spacesuit samples suggest
articles.dek: Tucked away among its sensors, cameras and navigation tools, NASA's Mars rover Perseverance is wearing small swatches of spacesuit material.
paragraphs: Tucked away among its sensors, cameras and navigation tools, NASA's Mars rover Perseverance is wearing small swatches of spacesuit material. A rover doesn't need a spacesuit, but the swatches—each less than a square inch (6. 5 square centimeters) in size—serve an important purpose: They're helping scientists assess the potential damage caused by ubiquitous Martian dust.

"Mars is a very dusty place," said Scott VanBommel, a research assistant professor of earth, environmental and planetary sciences in WashU Arts & Sciences. "Astronauts to Mars will have to be prepared."

VanBommel is the lead author of a new paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that examines how dust interacts with Perseverance's spacesuit swatches and other materials, including Teflon. Co-authors include Abigail Knight, a staff scientist who helped conceptualize and conduct the analysis as a Ph. D. student. Both researchers are also fellows of the McDonnell Center for the Space Sciences.

Planners of future Mars missions have good reason to plan around dust. On the Apollo missions, which were far shorter than any potential visit to Mars, lunar dust scratched visors and degraded spacesuits. When the astronauts returned to the lunar module, particles clinging to their suits contaminated the air and eventually entered their lungs, causing hay fever–like symptoms in some cases.

The new study suggests Martian dust may not be quite as abrasive or irritating as its lunar counterpart. The swatches showed little visible wear after 1,645 Martian days, an encouraging finding for future visitors.

Closer inspection revealed that particles on Mars were much smoother than the jagged grains found on the moon, suggesting they may be less likely to scratch equipment or irritate human lungs. "The particles in the Martian atmosphere have been blowing in the wind for potentially billions of years, so they tend to be well rounded, like pebbles in a river," VanBommel said.

But there's another problem: Martian dust can be exceptionally fine. VanBommel developed a method to estimate the size of each particle, some of which were ultrafine specks measuring as small as 100 nanometers (one ten-thousandth of a millimeter) across.

On Earth, ultrafine particles from smoke and other forms of air pollution pose a significant health threat because they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Astronauts won't breathe the Martian atmosphere directly, but engineers will need to account for these microscopic hazards when designing habitats, spacesuits and air filters, VanBommel said.
"The electrostatic properties of Martian dust are likely causing it to preferentially adhere to some surfaces," Knight added.

The data acquired by Perseverance's PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry) instrument also enabled the researchers to analyze the particles' chemical composition. Unlike lunar dust, the material on Mars contains perchlorates and other potentially toxic compounds. It's also enriched in sulfur, iron and silica.

Brief exposure to these substances may not seriously threaten astronauts' health; a lot comes down to dose and duration. Still, their presence adds another risk for mission planners to consider, VanBommel said.

Perseverance and previous rovers have given researchers remarkable insights into the history and current conditions on Mars. But beyond their scientific discoveries, these missions also serve as real-world tests of technology that could one day support human exploration.

"We've been operating rovers on the surface of Mars continuously for more than 20 years at this point," VanBommel said. "We know that dust will be a challenge, but it's something we can prepare for and overcome."
Journal information: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

articles.title: New restrictions kick in as Delhi battles pollution
articles.dek: Authorities in New Delhi stepped up anti-pollution measures on Sunday, including higher parking fees and work-from-home orders, seeking to curb toxic smog in one of the…
paragraphs: Authorities in New Delhi stepped up anti-pollution measures on Sunday, including higher parking fees and work-from-home orders, seeking to curb toxic smog in one of the world's most polluted capitals.

The restrictions, which came into force Sunday, include a doubling of vehicle parking charges and work-from-home arrangements for government and private-sector offices aimed at cutting traffic emissions.

Authorities will also bar vehicles that do not comply with mandated emission standards from entering the capital, while a ban on all dust-generating demolition and outdoor construction activity takes effect immediately.
"From Nov. 1 ... Delhi's Winter Action Plan comes into effect with stricter pollution controls, stronger enforcement and 24×7 monitoring," Chief Minister Rekha Gupta's office said in a statement.
"We humbly request all Delhiites to follow the guidelines and contribute toward making Delhi's air cleaner and healthier."
Delhi's government has already rolled out a range of pollution-control measures over the past month, including a ban on trash burning and restrictions on food stalls using coal or firewood.
But similar efforts in previous years have done little to prevent the annual smog that engulfs the megacity from November to January, when cooler temperatures trap pollutants close to the ground.
Major sources of pollution include vehicle emissions, coal-fired power plants, industrial activity, construction dust and the burning of crop residue in neighboring states.
Vehicles account for 23% of Delhi's winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20%, according to India's environment ministry.
Industry, including coal-fired power plants, contributes about 9%.

Levels of PM2. 5, tiny cancer-causing particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, frequently exceed 300 micrograms per cubic meter during peak winter months, around 20 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily limit.
Last year, pollution levels peaked at 846 micrograms per cubic meter, or 56 times the WHO guideline.
On Sunday, monitors recorded PM2. 5 at 201 micrograms per cubic meter, over 13 times the safe limit, a reading that was likely helped by intermittent rain over the last few days.
A 2024 study published in The Lancet Planetary Health estimated that 3. 8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution .

articles.title: 'Air-con nation' Singapore eyes alternatives to cool down
articles.dek: Long dubbed an "air-conditioned nation," Singapore is experimenting with cooling alternatives from chilled beams to "passive displacement" to curb its thirst for…
paragraphs: Long dubbed an "air-conditioned nation," Singapore is experimenting with cooling alternatives from chilled beams to "passive displacement" to curb its thirst for energy-guzzling air conditioning.
The city-state has the highest per capita air conditioner ownership rate in Southeast Asia, with about 99% of private residences equipped with cooling units.
Singapore's local building sector accounts for one-fifth of its emissions, while cooling itself accounts for 40% to 60% of a building's energy consumption, according to studies.

A stroll down renowned thoroughfare Orchard Road highlights that dependence. Shoppers are greeted by blasts of cool air that waft into the street as doors swing open—a major draw given daytime highs hover between 31C and 33C (88 to 91 degrees Fahrenheit) year-round.

But air conditioning can make the heat problem worse. Compressor units belch hot air back out into the environment, and the electricity that powers the systems can contribute to climate change if generated from fossil fuels.
Some buildings in Singapore are looking at other options, including active chilled beams, which are perforated panels equipped with cooling coils that are mounted on ceilings.
A chiller plant on the building's top floor cools water down to 9C (48 degrees Fahrenheit), then pumps it into the coils. Simultaneously, air is blasted through small nozzles inside the beams.
The jets of air create a low-pressure zone that sucks up warmer air from the room below so it passes over the coils and is cooled before recirculating.
The technology keeps the offices at the eight-story Paya Lebar Green building in eastern Singapore at a comfortable 24C (75 degrees Fahrenheit).
A visiting AFP team felt noticeably cooler air flowing from the sleek white panels on the ceiling of the building, described as one of Singapore's "greenest."
The system is also quiet, without the constant hum of air-conditioning units.

When HR professional Renuga Shekar first moved into an office space at Paya Lebar Green last November, the 30-year-old and her colleagues just thought the exposed pipes and panels on the ceiling were a "warehouse kind of look."
"We didn't really think much about it. No one really commented about it," she told AFP.
It was only months later, after noticing how quiet the office was and hearing technicians mention "ACB" during maintenance, that they realized it was cooled by active chilled beams.

articles.title: From Italy to Croatia, a warming climate threatens prized white truffles
articles.dek: Guided by the beam of a flashlight, Tino Marolo follows his dog Stella through the darkness of a Piedmont woodland, searching for one of Italy's most prized culinary…
paragraphs: Guided by the beam of a flashlight, Tino Marolo follows his dog Stella through the darkness of a Piedmont woodland, searching for one of Italy's most prized culinary treasures hidden beneath the soil.

In the hills around Alba, home to the world's most famous white truffles, hunters known as "trifolau" traditionally begin their season on Oct. 1. But increasingly, they are confronting a challenge above ground: climate change.
Months of heat and drought have raised concerns about the future of the prized white truffle, a fungus that depends on cool, moist soils and a delicate relationship with tree roots .

"The entire month of October was affected by the lack of rain in July and August and the high temperatures, so it was characterized by poor production and poor truffle shelf life," said Antonio Degiacomi, president of Italy's National Centre for Truffle Studies.
According to Degiacomi, dry and compacted soils have also produced smaller truffles this season.

The difficult harvest comes as Alba and the surrounding Langhe hills welcome visitors for the International White Truffle Fair, one of Italy's best-known food events, which opened on Oct. 10 and runs until Dec. 6.
For Axel Iberti, president of the fair, the season began slowly, with smaller truffles emerging after a hot, dry summer. More recent rains have improved conditions, helping larger specimens appear.

Despite tighter supplies, demand remains strong. Prices at Alba's truffle market are running about 20% to 30% higher than last year, Iberti said, while hotels and other accommodations have largely sold out during the fair period.
"This year certainly stands out from a trend we all know has been going on for five or six years now," Degiacomi said, citing hotter summers and increasingly erratic rainfall patterns.
Back in the woods, Marolo says uncertainty has always been part of the hunt.
"You certainly come home empty-handed more often than you do with a truffle," he said. "It's really the thrill of saying: I don't know what I'm going to find."
Similar concerns are emerging elsewhere in Europe's truffle-producing regions, suggesting a challenge extending beyond any single forest or region.
Across the Adriatic Sea in Croatia, truffle hunters and scientists describe many of the same challenges, from shrinking harvests to declining habitat suitability.
In oak forests outside Zagreb, truffle hunter Petar Alebic says years of drought have made the prized fungi harder to find.

articles.title: Warmer seas and shifting pressure systems: The signs that suggest the Mediterranean's climate is 'tropicalizing'
articles.dek: Nowhere in the Iberian Peninsula or the Balearic Islands has a tropical climate—for this to be the case, the average temperature in the coldest month would have to be 18°C…
paragraphs: Nowhere in the Iberian Peninsula or the Balearic Islands has a tropical climate—for this to be the case, the average temperature in the coldest month would have to be 18°C (64 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher. The contrast between Spain's winters and summers, and the low temperatures reached in winter, do not resemble those of any tropical climate.
However, over recent decades, climates across the Mediterranean basin have begun to show signs of tropicalization: the process of transitioning toward a tropical climate.
This is evident in several areas, including rising air and sea temperatures, shifting atmospheric patterns, and increasingly erratic rainfall.

First, a marked rise in air temperature —more pronounced than the global average—is making the Mediterranean's winters shorter and its summers longer, bringing spring forward and delaying the onset of autumn. Some people believe that these transitional seasons have all but disappeared. They do still exist, but they have moved on the calendar.
The temperature of shallow and deep Mediterranean water—down to a depth of around 100m (328 feet)—has also risen markedly.

These are clear, statistically significant trends. Water temperatures to the south of Mallorca exceeded 30°C (86 degrees Fahrenheit) on some days in recent summers. These temperatures are similar to, or even higher than, those found in the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.

The Northern Hemisphere's major wind belts and pressure systems, and the belt of tropical and subtropical high-pressure systems to the south of the Mediterranean basin—which cause the existence of the Sahara and other deserts at a similar latitude—all appear to be moving northward.
This is because of the expansion of the Hadley cell , a global-scale tropical atmospheric circulation that governs weather patterns at equatorial and tropical latitudes.

If this trend becomes established, it will increase atmospheric stability in the Mediterranean region. Rainfall would become less regular in the region, with long dry spells punctuated by heavy downpours.
Warm waters are one of the necessary ingredients for a hurricane to form and grow. Rising sea temperatures will therefore expand the areas of the ocean where such a phenomenon can potentially form.

For a hurricane to form, the minimum surface temperature—down to a depth of several tens of meters—has to be around 26. 5°C (79. 7 degrees Fahrenheit), a figure exceeded in large areas of the Mediterranean this summer. The abundant water vapor and the latent heat it carries provide the fuel for intense convective processes that generate storms, often resulting in torrential downpours.

For several decades now, atmospheric depressions have been developing in the Mediterranean with characteristics that are reminiscent of tropical cyclones. These are known as medicanes , "Mediterranean mini-hurricanes," or "Mediterranean tropical-like cyclones" .

articles.title: Why some trees thrive far from home—and what that means for carbon sinks
articles.dek: In a study spanning 192 sites and four continents, researchers have discovered that conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere grow up to four times faster and are more…
paragraphs: In a study spanning 192 sites and four continents, researchers have discovered that conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere grow up to four times faster and are more drought-resistant than those growing in their native ranges.
This rapid growth and resilience could make conifers a strong candidate for carbon storage, but there may also be drawbacks to planting trees outside their home turf.

University of Mississippi ecologist Stephen Brewer was among more than two dozen researchers across multiple continents who studied the growth rate of pines, spruces, firs, cedars and other conifers in their native and nonnative habitats. The group published its findings in Nature .

"That result is surprising because ecological theory predicts that there should be a trade-off between how fast a plant can grow and how tolerant it would be of stressful conditions," said Brewer, an Ole Miss professor of biology. "This is interesting to us because with the elevated carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere contributing to climate change , there's a desire or push for afforestation , or planting trees in areas where there weren't any before, as carbon sinks.
"For that to be effective, you want the trees to grow quickly and not die in droughts."

While the exact cause of the trees' increased resilience needs more study, the researchers found that Northern Hemisphere conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere had higher concentrations of carbohydrates, such as sugars and starches, that could be used to store energy during stressful seasons.

"This phenomenon of skipping the growth-stress tolerance trade-off is something crucial that this study is reporting," said Alex Fajardo, a researcher at the Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity and a professor at the University of Talca. "It is also valuable that we pursued finding the physiological mechanism responsible for this: an increase in carbon reserves needed for drought tolerance."
Although the findings position conifers as well suited for afforestation efforts, the researchers cautioned that more factors are involved.

"The easy answer to this question is to advocate for plantations with nonnative conifers that can both grow (quickly) and tolerate drought," Fajardo said. "However, this decision has some serious risks, as nonnative conifer plantations, particularly in the Southern Hemisphere, have come with high biodiversity and social costs."

Pines and Douglas firs, two of the trees researchers studied, do not naturally grow in the Southern Hemisphere, but they have been planted in countries including Chile, Brazil and South Africa as a part of the lumber industry for decades.
"The problem is, these pines are not necessarily staying in their plantations; they are actually expanding into natural, native habitats," Brewer said.

"In Brazil, it's escaping into what they call their Cerrado, which is a savanna, and it grows much faster there and just basically eliminates all the native vegetation. It's actually become a big problem."

articles.title: A Breakthrough in Magnetism Could Make Computer Chips Use Dramatically Less Energy
articles.dek: Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.
paragraphs: Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.

A promising class of materials could help dramatically reduce the electricity needed for computing, but a persistent problem has kept them out of computer chips. When these materials are made thin enough for modern electronics, the electrical and magnetic properties that make them valuable can disappear.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces ultrathin films of bismuth ferrite that retain their essential properties and develop an additional form of magnetism with potential advantages for future computing devices. The findings were published in Nature Materials .

Bismuth ferrite belongs to a class of materials called multiferroics, which have interconnected electrical and magnetic properties. Within their crystalline structures, positive and negative charges are displaced in opposite directions, creating electrical polarization. Applying a small voltage can reverse that polarization, allowing information to be stored as binary data (ones and zeros). Because the electrical and magnetic states are linked, the stored information could also be read magnetically, potentially enabling memory and logic devices that consume far less power.

The obstacle is a phenomenon known as the “dead layer” effect. When multiferroic films become extremely thin, their atomic structures and chemical environments can change enough to disrupt their functionality. At the same time, internal electric fields can destabilize their polarization. Together, these effects can eliminate the ferroelectric and magnetic behavior needed for electronic applications.

The Brown team addressed both problems by carefully engineering the layers surrounding the bismuth ferrite. First, they grew the material on dysprosium scandate, a rare earth-based crystalline substrate with a smaller lattice spacing than bismuth ferrite. The mismatch places the film under compressive strain, helping preserve the atomic arrangement required for its electrical and magnetic properties.

The researchers also incorporated a metallic layer that screens unwanted electric fields, preventing them from destabilizing the film’s polarization. With both effects controlled, bismuth ferrite remained functional even at thicknesses of only a few angstroms. An angstrom measures approximately four billionths of an inch.

“We’ve established that we can get rid of the dead layer,” said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. “We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want — down to a few angstroms — and it’s still ferroelectric, and it’s still magnetic.”

Beyond preserving the material’s original properties, the engineered structure enhanced its magnetic behavior. The researchers demonstrated that the thin film exhibits altermagnetism, a magnetic state with characteristics that could overcome some limitations of conventional magnetic materials.

“Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out,” Caretta said. “The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds — they can be fast, densely integrated, and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.”

These characteristics could eventually support faster, more densely packed electronic components while reducing energy consumption. Although the researchers have demonstrated the material’s properties rather than a finished computing device, the technique addresses a major barrier to incorporating multiferroics into practical chips, particularly as artificial intelligence increases demand for computing power.

“We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials,” Caretta said. “The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that’s useful — and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.”

articles.title: A Mysterious Explosion in Space Just Did Something Scientists Didn’t Expect
articles.dek: An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years.
paragraphs: An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. Its visible light became brighter than its host galaxy, and its X-ray emission unexpectedly intensified again weeks later.

An international research team believes the extraordinary behavior can be explained by the direction of the explosion’s powerful jet. Rather than pointing directly toward Earth, the jet was viewed from an angle that initially concealed its most energetic region. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , suggest that some exceptionally powerful stellar explosions may be difficult to recognize from their initial gamma-ray flashes alone.

NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the event, designated GRB 260310A, on March 10, 2026. Its initial burst of gamma rays lasted approximately 53 seconds and appeared to release relatively little energy. Over the following hours, however, its visible afterglow steadily grew brighter before eventually fading.

The contrast became even more pronounced at other wavelengths. Compared with samples of previously observed gamma-ray bursts, the event’s X-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the brightest 1%, while its radio emission placed it among the brightest 5%. Approximately three weeks after the explosion, the X-ray afterglow brightened again, remaining unusually luminous for more than a week and detectable for months.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” says co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

Gamma-ray bursts are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Many occur when massive stars collapse and launch narrow jets of matter traveling at nearly the speed of light. As these jets collide with surrounding gas, they generate afterglows that can be detected in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.

Astronomers typically observe the brightest gamma-ray flashes when a jet points almost directly at Earth. GRB 260310A appears to have been different. Its relatively weak initial emission, followed by an exceptionally bright afterglow, is consistent with a jet viewed from outside its most intensely beamed region.

“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” explains Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar and lead author of the study.

The researchers propose that the explosion produced a jet with a narrow, highly energetic core surrounded by a wider, slower outflow. From Earth’s viewing angle, the broader outer regions would dominate the early afterglow, while much of the core’s radiation would initially be directed elsewhere.

As the jet slowed, its emission became visible across a wider range of angles. Radiation from the energetic core could then reach Earth, potentially explaining the delayed increase in X-ray brightness. This structured jet model offers a possible explanation for the unusual observations, although the precise configuration remains uncertain.
“We looked at it from a side angle. As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

The delayed X-ray brightening was particularly difficult to explain. “That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalls Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. “This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”

To investigate the event, the international team, led by the ERC-funded BHianca group at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, combined observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA’s XMM-Newton, the Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Additional observations from Calar Alto Observatory detected the signature of a supernova, confirming that the gamma-ray burst accompanied the death of a massive star.

The team’s models indicate that the jet’s central region may have carried vastly more energy than the initial gamma-ray measurements suggested. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” notes Yang. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

articles.title: “Nearly Everybody Had Given Up” – Scientists Finally Solve a 60-Year Chemistry Mystery
articles.dek: After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.
paragraphs: After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.

Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form.

Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in Nature Chemistry , the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India.

The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products.

“The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk.

Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block.

Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples.

“Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig.

The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table.
The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

articles.title: Parents, let your kids eat as much candy as they want – less restriction could help reduce the urge to overeat
articles.dek: Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home…
paragraphs: Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets, to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats. But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume.

As a registered dietitian and mom of three, I understand the stress that comes with wanting to encourage healthy food choices without removing all the fun of childhood traditions. I also believe the answer to this dilemma may be simpler than the familiar back and forth of “Just one more piece of candy!” and “Haven’t you had enough already?”

Research suggests that by managing the candy inventory less and encouraging more autonomy around sweets, parents can help their kids practice tapping into their hunger and fullness cues , promoting a healthier relationship with food over time.

There is no question that some foods have greater nutritional value than others. A piece of cake – carrot cake included – will never provide the vitamins and minerals of a large garden salad. As a result, people often categorize different foods as “good” or “bad.”

The tendency to place food in two polarizing buckets can affect everything from what foods you purchase at the grocery store to the language you use to describe food. The problem is, “ good” and “bad” are moral concepts . When morality is consistently applied to food, a person’s relationship to food can become complicated. Instead of viewing food as fueling, it can become a measuring stick for whether your food choices are something to feel proud of or guilty about.

When a person’s inner monologue about food is preoccupied with whether it is good or bad for their health or diet plan, food choices can become less about enjoyment and more about their willpower to make the “right” decision at the grocery store and at mealtimes. Any guilt or shame that comes from this evaluation can spill over into what foods are served freely at home and which are restricted.

The idea of food restriction often sounds punishing. For parents and others who take care of children, food restriction often may simply be an attempt to limit sugary foods and introduce more fruits and vegetables.

But for kids, restricting certain foods may lead them to become preoccupied with those foods . They may be nagged by the knowledge that the foods adults often call “bad” are also the ones that are really delicious. What started as a simple candy rule can continue to influence a child’s relationship to food and eating long after the treats are gone.

Parents often approach food restriction in two different ways . In overt food restriction, kids are aware that their parents or guardians are limiting access to specific foods because they can see it or are told specific foods are off limits. In practice, this might mean the kids know candy is in the house but stored out of reach in the kitchen cupboards. Parents or caregivers who practice covert food restriction, on the other hand, may choose to not buy bags of candy at all in order to encourage more balanced food choices.

Research suggests that overt restriction can unintentionally increase kids’ interest in those restricted food items . That preoccupation may mean the child has a more difficult time listening to their fullness cues when presented with those foods. If bags of candy are usually stored out of reach, it may be tempting to eat more than just a few pieces when access is finally granted – and they may completely ignore any signs that their body is full.

Incorporating neutral language about food at mealtimes and encouraging kids to eat according to their own hunger and fullness cues can help them build trust in their bodies and improve family connection at the table. Taking the pressure off finishing all the food on the plate can instead place emphasis on savoring the sensory experience of each bite.

Eating according to internal cues is one part of intuitive eating , which aims to increase a person’s trust in their own body to signal when to start eating and when to stop. Kids can also benefit from this same framework, with some age-appropriate modifications.

The Satter Division of Responsibility in Feeding provides a simple, research-based approach to feeding kids in a way that avoids power struggles between kids and caretakers at the table. Developed by the Ellyn Satter Institute, a nonprofit focused on improving people’s relationship to food, the goal of the framework is to introduce intuitive eating in a kid-friendly way. When providing food through this approach, parents decide when and what food is served, while kids are in charge of deciding what and how much they eat from their plates. The emphasis is on helping kids eat according to their internal cues without pressuring them to eat specific foods.

Candy can be a part of the menu rotation in this feeding framework. Repeatedly exposing kids to a variety of foods, including sugary treats outside of special holidays or events, means no food becomes emphasized for being better or worse than another food – it is all simply food .

This approach can shift the conversation to how different foods affect their bodies in different ways: Some food – like candy – makes them run super fast, some foods grow their muscles, while other foods keep their eyes strong.

Regularly using neutral language to describe food and exposing kids to a variety of foods helps reduce the power that sugary treats have over their appetites. This doesn’t mean birthday cake, doughnuts and candy will no longer taste delicious. It simply means children can rest assured they will see their favorite treats again without the added urge to overconsume them.
If you’re interested in exploring how intuitive eating principles could change your child’s or your own relationship with food, here are a few practices you can try at home:

Involve children in menu planning and grocery shopping . Let your kids pick a treat to add to a few meals each week, and serve the treat with the rest of the food on the menu for that day. Presenting all food items at the same time on the plate – versus saving a dessert or treat for after the meal – visually reminds everyone that food does not have to be earned. Rather, each food nourishes their bodies in different ways.

Avoid commenting on what your kids eat . It can be tempting to praise a child when they choose to take a bite of the broccoli you’ve been encouraging for weeks. Praising kids for eating certain foods versus others can create a food hierarchy , leading them to think about food as a way to earn a reward instead of fueling their body.

Challenge your own relationship with food . Do you eat when you are hungry and stop when you are full? Do you restrict your own food cravings as a punishment, or do you struggle to control yourself when eating a treat you love? Kids are always watching, and your own food behaviors often speak louder than words.

Consider letting your kids indulge for a day . In my own family, I don’t limit how much candy my three kids eat on Halloween night. I won’t lie – they usually eat quite a bit. When they mention a stomachache afterward, we talk about how eating a lot of candy can make their bodies feel – without adding judgment. Their interest typically fades over the next few days while we continue to offer a piece of two with meals. Eventually the extras become props for elaborate trick-or-treat pretend play.
One day or evening of holiday eating does not define their health , but fun memories with friends and families can last a lifetime. So let them eat … candy!

articles.title: How permanent daylight saving time could affect schools
articles.dek: Sleep is fundamental to well-being. Decisions to end semiannual clock changes and remain on permanent daylight saving time (DST) in British Columbia , the Northwest…
paragraphs: Sleep is fundamental to well-being. Decisions to end semiannual clock changes and remain on permanent daylight saving time (DST) in British Columbia , the Northwest Territories , Alberta , Manitoba and northwestern Ontario have consequences for many Canadians due to potential sleep disruption.

The health risks of transitioning to DST , including increased heart attacks and fatal car accidents , have led most sleep and chronobiology experts , including the first author of this story , to advocate for ending seasonal clock changes in favor of permanent standard time .
Governments justify opting for DST to provide later daylight for a range of reasons, including facilitating evening activities , alignment with other areas and promoting health.
While permanent DST provides more daylight in the evening hours—something sometimes appealing for those with flexible schedules and access to outdoor spaces—it comes at the cost of later sunrises.
Being aware of the potential effects of permanent DST and how to mitigate these will be important for schools.
Due to the short winter days experienced in Canada, dawn will now occur later than the start times for many schools in many of the regions opting for permanent DST.

Communities to the north and west within a time zone will have sunrises later than 8 a. m. , or even later than 9 a. m. for a sizable portion of the school year. Grande Prairie, Alberta, will see sunrises in December and January after 10 a. m.
In the United States, the Sunshine Protection Act seeks to make daylight saving time permanent .
Because winter days are shorter in northern Canada areas than in the more southern United States, the negative consequences of the move to permanent DST will be more profound for Canadians.

A major concern around choosing the right clock for society has to do with our body's internal circadian clock . This circadian clock regulates our daily 24-hour rhythms, including our sleep-wake cycles. This clock naturally follows daylight, so as our days get shifted later with DST, our body rhythms also get shifted later .

One challenge that many people will face with permanent DST is social jetlag—a mismatch between what our body clock wants to do (follow the sun) and what our school or work schedules expect us to do (follow our alarm clocks).

DST worsens social jetlag in two ways. First, DST moves our social schedule an hour earlier relative to dawn. For people with earlier schedules, such as students and teachers, this means waking earlier than our bodies want with the later dawns during fall and winter. Second, later sunsets delay when our bodies want to fall asleep, leading to less sleep overall .

Social jetlag also erodes health in several ways, raising rates of depression, cardiovascular disease and metabolic diseases. How a person will respond to permanent DST depends on both their work or school schedule and their chronotype. Those with flexible schedules can adapt their sleep and activity schedules, but this isn't a luxury afforded to many.

articles.title: A Hidden DNA Mechanism Could Explain How 20% of Human Cancers Develop
articles.dek: Mutations found in roughly 20% of human cancers may promote tumor growth by changing how DNA is organized inside cells.
paragraphs: Mutations found in roughly 20% of human cancers may promote tumor growth by changing how DNA is organized inside cells. Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows a regulatory protein to reshape the genome’s three-dimensional structure, altering the activity of genes involved in cell division.

The study, published October 28 in Nature , links these changes to mutations affecting a protein complex called BAF. Scientists at Weill Cornell Medicine found that blocking a key protein involved in the process reversed the cancer-promoting effects in an animal model, suggesting potential new approaches to treatment.

The BAF complex helps control gene activity by regulating how accessible DNA is to other proteins. Its numerous subunits are encoded by more than two dozen genes, and mutations affecting these components occur in cancers of the breast, ovaries, liver, and lymphatic system. Until now, researchers had struggled to explain how such mutations could contribute to malignancy across so many different tissues.

The new findings challenge expectations about how BAF normally functions. “We normally think of the BAF complex as making DNA more accessible, and so we expected its loss to have the opposite effect,” Dr. Meydan said. “Instead, its loss made DNA more accessible to CTCF, with surprisingly far-reaching effects.”

CTCF helps organize DNA into distinct regions by establishing boundaries that influence which genes interact with regulatory elements. These interactions depend partly on how DNA folds and loops within the nucleus. When BAF activity is lost, CTCF gains access to sites that would normally be less accessible, potentially disrupting this intricate organization.

“The challenge for us was to find a potential cancer-promoting effect occurring across many different cell types and tissue models,” said Dr. Barisic, who is also the John P. Leonard, M. D. /Gwirtzman Family Research Scholar in Lymphoma.

Using several animal and cell models with impaired BAF function, the researchers discovered that CTCF binding increased at thousands of locations throughout the genome. This widespread change reorganized DNA loops and folds, disrupting normal connections between genes and the regulatory regions that control their activity. The resulting shifts in gene expression encouraged faster cell division.

Evidence from mouse experiments and human cancer patient data further supported CTCF’s involvement. In particular, disruptions affecting CTCF were associated with better patient outcomes. The researchers also demonstrated that deleting CTCF in an animal model could reverse the effects of BAF mutations, providing experimental evidence that the protein contributes to the cancer-promoting process.

The team identified two additional protein complexes, PBAF and ISWI, that cooperate with CTCF in driving these changes. Removing either complex also blocked the effects of BAF mutations in experimental models, making all three potential targets for future therapies.

“These findings help us establish a unifying mechanism for one of the most common classes of cancer mutations, and identify CTCF and its partner proteins as candidate therapeutic targets in these cancers,” said study co-corresponding author Dr. Darko Barisic, an assistant professor of cancer biology in medicine and a member of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.

Although the experiments identify promising molecular targets, researchers have not yet established whether blocking these proteins can safely treat cancer in humans. The next challenge is understanding precisely how increased CTCF binding changes the genome and finding ways to interfere with that process.
“We’re currently investigating in more detail what this extensive gain of CTCF does to the genome, and we hope before long to find a drug that blocks this process,” Dr. Barisic said.

articles.title: Can Cats Really Go Vegan? New Research Reveals a Surprising Health Connection
articles.dek: More cat owners are turning to vegan diets for their pets. But is a plant-based diet actually safe for cats?
paragraphs: More cat owners are turning to vegan diets for their pets. But is a plant-based diet actually safe for cats?
An online survey of 1,305 cats found that those eating vegan diets had 34% lower odds of being assessed as overweight than those eating conventional meat-based food.

The findings came from caregiver reports of veterinary assessments. All cats had followed their diets for at least one year, with conventional meat-based diets accounting for most (90%) and vegan diets for the remainder (10%).
Researchers calculated the difference after accounting for age, sex, neuter status, activity, and feeding practices.

The lower rates of excess weight came despite feeding habits that might have tipped the scales the other way, as Knight explained, “Interestingly, most vegan-fed cats were eating predominantly dry food and were more likely to have food available throughout the day. These are feeding patterns normally associated with increased overweight risk. Yet we still observed lower rates of overweight in this group.”

That observation came from study author Andrew Knight, an adjunct professor at Australia’s Griffith University School of Environment and Science. He emphasized that the relatively small vegan-fed group limited what researchers could conclude.

Veterinary studies estimate that around 30–60% of domestic cats are overweight or obese. Excess weight is associated with arthritis, diabetes, urinary tract disease, and reduced quality of life, giving researchers a reason to investigate dietary patterns that might help.

Caregivers of vegan-fed cats reported fewer weight-related disorders, with no cases reported for several conditions examined. However, the small number of cats in this group made those results uncertain.

“Carers feeding cats vegan diets also reported lower rates of body weight-related disorders such as osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal and mobility problems,” Knight said. “However, the relatively small number of vegan-fed cats means these results cannot be considered conclusive.”

The survey could not establish why vegan-fed cats appeared less likely to be overweight. Researchers did not analyze the foods themselves, so explanations involving their ingredients or nutritional composition remain possibilities.

Some commercial vegan cat foods may provide more fiber and fewer calories or less fat than comparable meat-based products, potentially supporting weight control. Differences in L-carnitine, a nutrient involved in energy metabolism and maintaining lean body tissue, could also contribute.

The results do not establish that avoiding meat prevents excess weight. Determining whether the diets themselves explain the pattern would require direct measurements of food consumption, calorie intake, and body condition over time.
Knight said the findings provide a reason for further investigation, rather than a definitive answer about vegan diets and feline weight.

“We can’t conclude from this study that vegan diets definitely protect cats against becoming overweight, but we have found a consistent pattern that is worth further investigation. An ideal next step would be a larger, prospective study that directly measured what cats are eating, their energy intake, and their body condition.”

articles.title: A Nutrient Found in Red Meat Could Make Dangerous Inflammation Even Worse
articles.dek: A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.
paragraphs: A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.

Yale researchers found that L-carnitine, a nutrient abundant in red meat and widely used in exercise and weight-loss supplements, could worsen severe inflammation in mice. After a bacterial component triggered inflammation and sharply lowered blood levels of L-carnitine, restoring the nutrient made the animals sicker, suggesting the decline was protective.
L-carnitine is best known for helping cells turn fat into energy. The body produces it naturally, and skeletal muscle contains particularly high concentrations.

“L-carnitine helps transport fats into mitochondria so they can be broken down for energy,” says Eric Elliott, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and the study’s first author. “In simpler terms, it has become synonymous with fat burning, which is why it has also gained prominence as an exercise and weight-loss supplement.”

The team was investigating metabolic changes during sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to infection damages its own tissues and organs. Much of that damage can come from uncontrolled inflammation rather than a failure to contain the infection.

“Sepsis is incredibly challenging,” Elliott says. “Patients with sepsis can become critically ill, and among patients with sepsis treated in intensive care units, some studies report mortality rates approaching 40%.”

To model the inflammation associated with sepsis, the researchers exposed mice to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial component. When L-carnitine levels in the animals’ blood dropped sharply, the team tested whether restoring the nutrient would improve their outcomes.
“We predicted giving carnitine back to these animals might improve their outcomes, but they actually did much worse,” Elliott says. “That told us the reduction in carnitine was an adaptive response.”

To understand why, the researchers conducted experiments in mouse and human immune cells. They found that L-carnitine activated part of the cell’s internal alarm system called the pyrin inflammasome. This triggered an inflammatory response involving the immune signaling molecule IL-17 and increased deaths among the mice.

“What was particularly striking was how detrimental IL-17 was in this model,” Elliott says. The team now wants to investigate whether blocking IL-17 might eventually help a subset of patients with sepsis, although that possibility remains untested.

The findings offer a potential research direction in a field where treatment advances have been limited. “We have made frustratingly little progress in improving sepsis treatment beyond learning how to better deliver fluids, antibiotics, and medications that support blood pressure,” Elliott says.

Because skeletal muscle contains high levels of L-carnitine, the researchers suspected that its release from damaged muscle could help drive inflammation. Senior author Andrew Wang, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine (rheumatology, allergy & immunology) and of immunobiology at YSM, says the pathway may have implications beyond sepsis.

“There is tantalizing genetic evidence that the pathway we uncovered could be contributing to inflammation in a variety of diseases, particularly diseases in which muscle involvement has perhaps been thought to be a casualty of the disease rather than a potential driver,” Wang says.

The team found support for this idea in rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which skeletal muscle rapidly breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially causing acute kidney injury. In a mouse model, L-carnitine transport and pyrin inflammasome activation contributed to inflammation, suggesting that immune cells may interpret L-carnitine released from damaged muscle as a warning signal.

articles.title: New X-Ray Technology Captures 4.6 Times More Light Without Losing Sharpness
articles.dek: Scientists have developed a new approach to X-ray imaging that captures significantly more light without sacrificing image sharpness.
paragraphs: Scientists have developed a new approach to X-ray imaging that captures significantly more light without sacrificing image sharpness.

A major obstacle to sharper X-ray images is that much of the light generated inside detectors never reaches the camera. Researchers have developed a nanostructured surface that increased average light output by 4. 64 times and improved the imaging signal-to-noise ratio by 13 decibels. The experimental system also maintained spatial resolution finer than 25 μm (about 0. 001 inch).

Developed by scientists at Chongqing University, the 26th Institute of CETC, and Stevens Institute of Technology, the approach could help X-ray detectors produce clearer images when very few photons are available. Potential applications include medical scans using lower radiation doses, security screening, and detailed industrial inspections.

X-ray imaging relies on materials called scintillators to convert invisible X-ray radiation into visible light. These “photosensitive” components act as a “translator,” converting the “language” of high-energy radiation into optical signals that cameras or photodetectors can capture and turn into images.

High-density inorganic scintillators (such as GAGG) are particularly effective at absorbing X-rays and generating light, but much of that light cannot escape. Because these materials have a substantially higher refractive index than their surroundings, light striking the surface at certain angles undergoes total internal reflection. Up to 90% of the generated photons can become trapped in guided optical modes, reducing the amount of light available for imaging.

This problem becomes more severe when detectors operate with weak X-ray signals. Increasing scintillator thickness can improve X-ray absorption, but it also allows light to spread sideways before detection, reducing image sharpness. Thinner scintillators preserve fine details but can produce weaker signals.

The researchers addressed this trade-off by modifying how light escapes the scintillator rather than increasing its thickness. Their design uses a photonic crystal, a regularly repeating nanoscale structure that changes how light travels through a material.

Through a process known as Bragg diffraction, the periodic structure provides additional momentum that allows previously trapped light to escape into free space. This increases the amount of visible light reaching the detector without requiring a thicker scintillator.

Manufacturing such structures over large areas has been difficult. Conventional lithography offers precise patterning but requires costly equipment and complicated processing, particularly on brittle scintillator surfaces. Simpler self-assembly techniques can cover larger areas, but cracks, missing particles, and poorly aligned crystal regions can reduce light extraction and introduce imaging artifacts.

The team developed a self-assembly technique that uses the Marangoni effect, in which differences in surface tension drive liquid movement. By combining ethanol and water, the researchers created surface tension gradients that helped organize polystyrene nanospheres into a highly ordered layer.

Surfactants helped pack the particles more tightly, while a vibration-free drainage process transferred the assembled structure onto a 25 mm (about 0. 98 inch) diameter GAGG scintillator wafer. The resulting photonic crystal consisted of a continuous monolayer of nanospheres arranged in a hexagonal close-packed pattern.

The research was led by Associate Professor Feng Peng of Chongqing University, working with Dr. Ding Yuchong of the 26th Institute of CETC and PhD candidate Kaifeng Liu of Stevens Institute of Technology. Their paper was published in Opto-Electronic Advances .

The experimental findings demonstrate that modifying the scintillator surface can substantially improve light extraction while preserving fine image details. This approach could be particularly useful in photon-starved conditions, where limited X-ray exposure makes it difficult to distinguish weak signals from background noise.

Further development is still needed before the technology can be widely adopted. Residual structural defects can affect spatial resolution, and the researchers plan to refine the assembly process and investigate compatibility with other scintillator materials.

articles.title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
articles.dek: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated…
paragraphs: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “ The Last of Us ,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “ SpongeBob SquarePants .”

These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close.

I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.

Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making.
The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus , Ophiocordyceps , which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”

The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin.

Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip . After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again.

How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers , but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.

The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus , showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it.

Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved.

That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus.
Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior.

The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa , uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it.

Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed.

Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.

Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.
Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. Toxoplasma gondii can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats.

While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even become attracted to cat odors . This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.

These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator.

There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.

So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them.
Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.
Tara Deans receives funding from the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: NASA Releases MAX POWER Key Events for Media, Participants
articles.dek: America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov.
paragraphs: America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER , NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recent Inspiration Tour , which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft.
A current schedule of events is available on the agency’s website .

MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a. m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8.

NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p. m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, the Moon Base is humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration.
Live coverage of the news conference will stream on a variety of platforms online. Learn where to watch:

Media credentialing for this event is closed. Media approved for this event must request interviews in advance. Space in the news conference is limited, and first come, first served. Media also may participate in the news conference virtually. To request call details or an interview, please contact Lauren Low in the NASA Headquarters newsroom at: lauren. e. low@nasa. gov .

articles.title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
articles.dek: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U. S.
paragraphs: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U. S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions , lawsuits and state action . But as a political scientist who studies election law , I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “ Spurious Ticket .”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted , recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy , no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery , but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan , the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives , and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation . This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters . In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

articles.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
articles.dek: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.
paragraphs: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”

The Request for Information seeks commercial interest in: potentially conducting a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime; servicing Hubble to enhance its capabilities; or performing a safe, controlled re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble’s mission.

“Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”
The Request for Information is available online and will remain open for responses until 3 p. m. EST, Monday, Nov. 30.

Like all spacecraft in low Earth orbit, Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing over time because of atmospheric drag. Hubble does not have a propulsion system to maintain its own orbit, and analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As such, NASA anticipates that a mission would need to take place by 2032.

The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for more than three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.
